summary: feat(core): add hooks, the external command hook runner — craft has offered a hooks:provide permission and a HookFiles accessor since it landed and nothing anywhere parsed or ran a hooks.json, a seam with no consumer, so the runner lands in core, where the platform owns it: hooks.json decodes to Group{Matcher, Hooks} and Hook{Type, Command, Timeout}, the primary file is loaded trusted while extra sources are untrusted by default and LoadWithSources skips a source that cannot be read or parsed while a broken primary file stays fatal, and an unknown event name or an empty command is rejected instead of silently never firing; Manager.Fire runs every matching group synchronously and returns no error, because a hook that times out, exits non-zero or cannot start is logged and skipped — user hooks are advisory, and an agent loop must not stop because a script broke; the runner builds the stdin event object and stamps 'event' itself instead of trusting the producer, never mutating the producer's map, and an untrusted source loses the content fields (tool inputs, tool results, prompts, commands, errors, messages, targets) before the command runs; three hardening upgrades over the reference implementation each carry a test that fails without it: a timeout kills the process group rather than the shell (sh -c wraps the real work, so killing sh alone leaves the descendants running — Setpgid plus kill(-pgid) with SIGKILL on Unix, documented as child-only on Windows), WaitDelay bounds the wait for the output pipe a hook's background process would otherwise hold for 25s+ (ErrWaitDelay is reported as 'output pipe left open', not as a hook failure), and the 64 KiB log capture is a locked, bounded writer because exec copies stdout and stderr from separate goroutines into the same writer; Observer is the in-core producer — a claimed kanban card fires SubagentStart and a terminal one SubagentStop, wired through core/event so any application that builds a delegation board gets the subagent events — and the resource factories hooks.Runner and hooks.SubagentObserver (ImplLocal) take plugin sources either as a factory option (WithSources, asked on every build) or as a document dependency (WithSourceDep, whose dep name and contract the host supplies, because core does not name craft's contract), with the observer subscribing in Wire per resource.Wireable; the executing tests skip on Windows, which needs a POSIX shell and a process-group kill, while that lane still builds and vets the package; feat(core): add utils/lock, a crash-safe single-instance lock — an O_EXCL pid file cannot survive a crash, because the file stays behind and the next launch reads it as occupied until the user finds and deletes it by hand, so Acquire takes a non-blocking advisory exclusive lock (flock on Unix, LockFileEx on Windows) on a file whose contents are a JSON holder record — pid, kind, start time, version, optional endpoint — that is diagnostics rather than authority, and returns a HeldError carrying the parsed record so a caller can tell a live holder from an unusable path, with IsHeld peeling that out of a wrapped error chain and ReadInfo reading the record without attempting the lock at all; sharing is opt-in because flock hands a second caller the first caller's lock, which would silently turn the take into a no-op (ShareWithinProcess is for callers that mean it — a workspace lock where a GUI and the agents it spawns are one logical user); Release unlocks and keeps the file, since removing it would let a third process lock a fresh inode while the old one is still held, splitting one lock into two; on Windows the lock covers a byte 1 GiB into the file rather than the record at offset 0, because a Windows range lock is enforced rather than advisory, so locking the bytes a diagnostics reader needs makes every one of those reads fail with ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION; and a record that does not parse — a bare pid line from the O_EXCL era, a truncated write after a crash — never blocks the takeover, reading as an unknown holder rather than as held; fix(core): move the HTTP/2 client and the MITM server off the x/net APIs v0.60.0 deprecated, which the whole-module lint gate would otherwise report as seven SA1019s — the HTTP/2 transport is the standard library's now (the cloned default transport keeps ForceAttemptHTTP2, so ALPN negotiates h2, and HTTP2Config takes the health-check knobs field for field, with PingInterval mapping to SendPingTimeout plus PingTimeout and WriteByteTimeout, while IdleConnTimeout moves to Transport.IdleConnTimeout), and the reachable HTTP/2 code is the toolchain's own copy, which the vulnerability scan follows; the MITM engine's h2 branch runs through a real http.Server over the single-connection listener the HTTP/1.1 path already uses, with the server reading the client's ALPN choice off the connection so the handshake stays ours and request contexts are tied to the client connection here too, cancelling an in-flight upstream request when the client disconnects; Transport writes NextProtos into the config it is handed, so NewRoundTripper gives each transport a clone — one config shared by an HTTP/2 and an HTTP/1.1 client otherwise leaves the HTTP/1.1 client offering h2, which the new protocol-selection test catches — and new tests cover the Config-to-HTTP2Config mapping and an end-to-end HTTP/2 round trip through the MITM engine; fix(core): raise the module floor to Go 1.26.0 and golang.org/x/net to v0.60.0 for the Go security batch published on 2026-10-08 (GO-2026-6603, -6607, -6608, -6611, -6612, -6613 and -6617 fix the standard library in go1.26.9 and go1.27.2 only, with no 1.25 release for any of them, and the x/net half is fixed in v0.60.0, which declares go 1.26.0 itself), together with the rest of the tidy result (x/sys v0.48.0, x/text v0.42.0, x/sync v0.23.0, x/mod v0.41.0); feat(core/runtime): default a dynamic agent removal to the document's bound — the drain bound was per call only, so every call site repeated it, and runtime.agents.remove_timeout is now strictly decoded, must be positive, and is applied by UnregisterAgent when the call gives no WithRemoveTimeout (WithRemoveTimeout, then the document's bound, then the caller's context), with the bound riding its generation through a reload and Runtime.AgentRemoveTimeout reporting it so wrappers such as craft's SyncAgents can fall back to it; this tag also carries the test-only fix that escapes the paths the hook tests splice into JSON, which is what keeps the core Windows lane green.
